draft.title: Long-term causes of the First World War
card: Militarism
Great powers built up large armies and navies and planned for war. Britain and Germany raced to build more warships.
Rival alliances
Europe split into two armed groups of countries that promised to support each other. A quarrel between two states could pull in their partners.
Imperial competition
Powers competed for colonies, trade and resources in Africa and Asia. This caused rivalry and distrust between them.
Nationalism
Strong pride in one's own nation, and in some places the wish of a people to rule themselves, led to rivalry between states and to unrest within empires.
draft.remember: Four pressures built tension in Europe before 1914: arms, alliances, empires and national pride.

a.q: Britain and Germany each built more warships to keep up with the other. Which long-term cause does this show?
a.why: Building up armed forces and planning for war is militarism. Alliances are promises of support between countries, which is a different idea, even though both sides in an arms race had allies.

b.q: In the 1890s, a European power sent troops to claim land in Africa. Another power did the same, and each accused the other of stealing. Which cause does this best show?
b.why: The two powers were rivals over colonies, which is imperial competition. Troops were used, but the dispute was about gaining territory, not about building up armed forces in Europe, so militarism is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: What were the two powers fighting over?

proposal.remember: Four pressures built tension in Europe before 1914: arms, alliances, empires and national pride.

a.q: Before 1914, many Poles living under Russian rule wanted a separate Polish state. Which long-term cause does this show?
a.why: A people wanting to rule themselves in their own state is nationalism, and it caused unrest within empires. Russia was an empire, but this is not great powers competing for colonies abroad, so imperial competition is wrong.
a.clue: Who wants change here: a great power or a people?
